Computers and the Superfold

Alexander R. Galloway New York University

Abstract Could it be that Deleuzes most lasting legacy will lie in his Postscript on Control Societies, a mere 2,300-word essay from 1990? While he discussed computers and new media infrequently, Deleuze admittedly made contributions to the contemporary discourse on computing, cybernetics and networks, particularly in his late work. From the concepts of the rhizome and the virtual, to his occasional interjections on the digital versus the analogue, there is a case to be made that the late Deleuze has not only inuenced todays discourse on new media but also proposes an original set of arguments about society and politics at the turn of the new millennium. Focusing on the Postscript on Control Societies and a handful of texts that surround it, we will reconstruct an image of what it means to live in the information age. This will have consequences for how we dene the digital and the analogue, what the computer means, and ultimately provide some insight into one of the more elusive terms in all of Deleuze, the superfold. Keywords: computer, control, digital, information age, capitalism, superfold Could it be? Could it be that Deleuzes most lasting legacy will consist of 2,300 words from 1990? Such a strange little text, his Postscript on Control Societies (Deleuze 1995b: 17782). It bears not the same Deleuzian voice so familiar from his other writings. Cynics will grumble it falls short of the great books of 19689 or the radical collaborations with Félix Guattari during the 1970s.1 A different voice resonates here, a more directly political voice, and barring the Guattari collaborations a voice less commonly heard in Deleuzes writings. Deleuze was always

Deleuze Studies 6.4 (2012): 513528 DOI: 10.3366/dls.2012.0080 © Edinburgh University Press www.eupjournals.com/dls

514 Alexander R. Galloway

a political thinker, certainly, and remained politically committed in various ways throughout his life. But the Postscript is different. Today, I can say that I feel completely Marxist, he admitted in a late interview published posthumously (1995a). The article I published on the society of control, for example, is completely Marxist, even though I am writing on things that Marx knew nothing about.2 Indeed in the article he indicts capitalism by name. He raises his wrath against corporations and television shows. But not just the mode of production, his frame is the culture at large. He talks about snakes and surfers and other features of the dawning millennium. He references Roberto Rossellini, Paul Virilio, Franz Kafka and most importantly Michel Foucault. He tells us exactly what is wrong with the business sector, as well as with the prisons, schools and hospitals. It reads almost like a manifesto, the Manifesto on Control Societies. Manifestos are always about two things: the desires and the details. This is what we want; and we want it here, and in this manner. When the May 1968 revolts broke out in France, Philippe Sollers, along with Julia Kristeva, Jean-Joseph Goux, Jean-Louis Baudry and a band of other signatories, wrote La révolution ici maintenant: sept points, listing their grievances, point by point (Baudry et al. 1968). And they added at the end we shall meet on Wednesdays at nine oclock on the rue de Rennes. This is the crux of the cahiers de doléances refrain, reprised recently in the closing sections of Michael Hardt and Antonio Negris Multitude: say what you want, and be specic about it. The year of Deleuzes death, 1995 was a good year for the manifesto. The Unabombers Industrial Society and the Future advocated the complete destruction of what he called the industrial-technological system. The Dogme 95 Vow of Chastity signed by lmmakers Lars Von Trier and Thomas Vinterberg that same year offered the closest thing to a manifesto seen in the cinema for some time. The Vow is as short as the Unabombers is long, but it is detailed, detailed, detailed. One must lm on location, in colour, on Academy 35mm stock and with concurrent diegetic sound. Ten years earlier, a computer engineer named Richard Stallman wrote the GNU Manifesto. The number of legitimate manifestos written by computer geeks can be counted on one hand the VNS Matrix Cyberfeminist Manifesto and Eben Moglens The dotCommunist Manifesto also come to mind. But despite its inauspicious source, Stallmans document had profound effects on the industrial-technological system, and almost all of them good. Detailed, like the others, Stallmans manifesto calls for the creation of a free Unix-compatible software

Computers and the Superfold 515

system, including a C compiler and a linker, a text editor and a few dozen other free software applications. He names the make and model of the computer his system will run on. He rebuts, pre-emptively, eleven specic objections raised by his would-be critics. (In a passage he might regret today, Stallman even calls for a software tax to underwrite the development of free code.) Most importantly, the manifesto calls for a stay free legal armature for copyright holders, known today as the GNU General Public License. Such was the intellectual climate that produced the Postscript on Control Societies. No computer-savvy intellectual was Deleuze. He likely had never heard of Stallmans manifesto much less read it. Nevertheless, scattered across his oeuvre, and particularly in his late work, Deleuze has unwittingly made signicant contributions to the contemporary discourse on computing, cybernetics and networks. From the concepts of the rhizome and the virtual, to his occasional interjections on the digital versus the analogue, and here with the notion of control society, there is a case to be made that Deleuze, while rarely mentioning computers directly, has dramatically inuenced todays discourse on new media. One of the most inuential aspects of the Postscript, particularly to my own thinking, is how it asserts so trenchantly that things are not getting any better. Computers are a curse not a panacea. Planetary neoliberalism is a boondoggle not a deliverance. The snake is even worse than the mole. For critics working in the shadow of the dot-com boom, such offerings from Deleuze furnished a welcome dose of fuel needed to combat the naïve utopian babble of the California ideology. Deleuze was always good at drawing lines in the sand. One of the things that make Deleuze such a pleasure to read is his clear construal of the theatre of enemies. They are excellent enemies. Not just information technologies and the life sciences, but Plato, Hegel and Descartes elite enemies, all of whom have committed the most egregious error. Each of these philosophical enemies has assented to the classical condition of philosophy. Each admits to an up-down distinction between idea and matter, between essence and instance, between Being and beings. The Postscript does not draw the line so much in terms of metaphysics. Here rather the complaint is articulated in terms of control, communication and the harshest connement wrought by the new monster of information society (Deleuze 1995b: 178). Deleuze credits the term to William Burroughs, but the true source for control is no mystery.3 Follow a thread from nineteenth-century thermodynamics and uid dynamics through statistical mathematics, weather prediction and

516 Alexander R. Galloway

nonlinear systems to terminate in 1948 with Norbert Wiener and his book Cybernetics: or Control and Communication in the Animal and the Machine. Then, stemming from Wiener and his brethren in the militaryindustrial research parks, follow the thread that leads through the rest of the twentieth century by way of systems theory, cellular automata and chaos theory. So why not call Deleuzes adversary by its true name?: the enemy is cybernetics. To describe the Postscript as a manifesto is to invoke the question of philosophical genre. An author may adopt different textual strategies to achieve different ends. The interview, the seminar, the essay, the book, these all demand different things from the philosopher, and command different participation by the reader. Of course the Postscript is no users manual on how to live; it is no call to action. It is no introduction to the non-fascist life, as Foucault said of Anti-Oedipus. Yet one can discern here some of the most basic requirements of a manifesto, these being an enumeration of grievances and a sermon for how to remedy them. But the question of philosophical genre can also be approached from another point of view. For is this short essay not dare I say a less philosophical Deleuze? The Postscript reveals a slightly more casual philosopher. It reveals a man more willing to comment about the current state of the world and its daily goings-on. Here is a thinker who is willing to make a hard and fast historical periodisation. Foucaults inuence is dramatic. Indeed the Postscript presents the kind of thinking more often seen in the writings of sociologists, political economists or even certain kinds of historians modes of writing none of which are classic Deleuze. He is expanding his normal repertoire to include a very clear argument about historical periodisation. The argument is no secret: at some point during the middle to late twentieth century disciplinary societies, characterised by connement and bureaucratic hierarchy, gave way to control societies, characterised by free-oating cybernetic organisation. Make no mistake, the gambit in the Postscript is larger than what might be evident at rst glance. In order to accept the concept of the control society, one must come to terms with a whole host of related concepts that, while not necessarily synonymous with control society, are nevertheless similar enough to demonstrate the success of the periodisation of the contemporary as such. In other words, to accept control society one must accept Jean-François Lyotards postmodern, Hardt and Negris empire, Manuel Castellss information age, Luc Boltanski and Ève Chiapellos new spirit of capitalism, and all the other related periodisation concepts. These various historical labels do

Computers and the Superfold 517

not mean the same thing, and they do not refer precisely to the same historical periods. But the ubiquity of such periodisation is evidence that something else is happening. The ubiquity of periodisation proves there exists a strong desire to theorise the last few decades as dramatically different from the high water mark of modernity. And further: that periodisation itself is something that ought to be done. People are free to squabble over this or that denition, nevertheless the Postscript demonstrates that periodisation is something that denes todays mode of being, whether or not people can agree on the historical periods themselves or what they might mean. Deleuze evokes many specic things in the Postscript that are notable, a few of which will be listed briey before expanding on one particular salient detail. A number of memorable images jump out to the reader: the ultrarapid forms of apparently free-oating control (les formes ultra-rapides de contrôle à lair libre); the sieve whose mesh varies from one point to another; big business as a soul, a gas; the fact that Surng has taken over from all the old sports; the passive danger of entropy and the active danger of sabotage; the mushrooming shantytowns and ghettos; and the dynamic between the moles burrow and the snakes coils (Deleuze 1995b: 17882).4 Likewise the Postscript is one of the few places where Deleuze mentions his intriguing concept of the dividual, a new kind of subject that emerges after the death of the individual. But the crux of the Postscript is something else entirely. The crux of this short text has to do with technology. For here is one of those rare moments in which Deleuze comments on actually existing contemporary technology, specically computers. Control societies, he writes, function with a third generation of machines, with information technology and computers (Deleuze 1995b: 180). Admittedly Deleuze does not delve too deeply into the specicities of computing. He is no Friedrich Kittler, or Geert Lovink, or McKenzie Wark. But in a way that perhaps nevertheless still trumps these other authors, Deleuze says a few brief words about an important pairing, the analogue and the digital. Not as broadly integrated into Deleuzes overall project as, say, the concept of the virtual, the analogue and the digital still gure importantly here. The following are the relevant sentences, which Deleuze uses to launch section two of the essay under the heading Logic (Logique, a cognate with the French word for software, logiciel):

The various placements or sites of connement through which individuals pass are independent variables: were supposed to start over each time at

518 Alexander R. Galloway

zero, and although all these sites have a common language, its analogical. The different forms of control, on the other hand, are inseparable variations, forming a system of varying geometry whose language is digital (though not necessarily binary). (Deleuze 1995b: 178; translation modied)

Only a passing reference, it is true, but still an important return to two terms that had appeared in Deleuzes philosophy for several years already. By way of background, go back to a text from his aesthetic period, the slim and elegant Francis Bacon: The Logic of Sensation (Deleuze 2004), which rst appeared in 1981.5 The book on Francis Bacon is of course not about the digital, nor is it about control society per se. But nevertheless Deleuze nds time in the monograph to pause for a moment and offer a few remarks on the digital and the analogue. As many people are want to do, Deleuzes rst instinct is to connect the digital to the universe of computation and code. Digital synthesizers, he writes qualifying them as audio synthesizers, but we might extrapolate his observations to include video synthesizers as well Digital synthesizers... are integral: their operation passes through a codication, through a homogenization and binarization of the data (Deleuze 2004: 95). The integral, integration, these are important concepts in Deleuzes work. Drawing on the use of the term in both mathematics and Freudian psychoanalysis, Deleuze uses integration to mean the actualisation of the virtual. Four terms are synonymous, he wrote a decade earlier in Difference and Repetition, actualise, differenciate, integrate and solve (Deleuze 1994: 211). To integrate a mathematical function means to nd the area under the curve. For example, one might integrate from a to b on the function f(x), meaning that, given the curve plotted of the function f(x), one sums the area under the curve bounded by x = a to x = b. At the same time the appeal for Deleuze is, I think, not so much the mathematical sources of the term integration but the curvilinear sources, shall we say the baroque sources. Curves are complex. Given the complexity of a curve, to solve a curve mathematically is something of a miracle. In fact such a feat eluded the ancients; it took the baroque mathematicians G. W. Leibniz and Isaac Newton to do it. As readers of Deleuze will already know, his ontology is one that posits an innite plane of heterogeneous elements, and on this plane the heterogeneous elements come to integrate themselves into more or less homogenous regularities of aggregation, comportment and association. Hence integration is a synonym for coordination or organisation in Deleuze. Integration is the miracle of givenness, and the subsequent management of those

Computers and the Superfold 519

given beings. Integration produces things like species, compositions and societies. And, lest we forget, the countervailing force exists as well, homogenous regularities that deterritorialise into the virtual, thereby suspending their specicity in favour of adjacent possibility spaces although Deleuze himself disliked the term possible. In the previously cited quotation from Francis Bacon, Deleuze more or less equates ve terms: digitisation, integration, codication, homogenisation and binarisation. Binarisation, the grouping of things into twos, is the same as digitisation, the separating or making distinct of things, is the same as integration, the solving of complex function curves, is the same as codication, the representation within a symbolic system, is the same as homogenisation, the making uniform of dissimilar ingredients. Needless to say the comparison of these ve terms raises a number of questions, not all of which will be resolved here. What is important, for Deleuze and for us, is that the digital is a transformative process (which is to say additive, or in Kantian vocabulary synthetic) in which a universe grounded in the univocity of an identity of the same becomes a universe grounded in discrete distinctions between elements, elements that, although divided, are brought together and held in relation, suspended opposite each other like cliffs over the banks of a great river. In the very same passage from Francis Bacon, Deleuze also says a few words, precious few, about the analogical. Not so much a question of code, the analogical is a question of diagram or motif. What this means is that the analogical operates in the realms of shape and relation, refrains and styles, not symbol or language in the classical sense. Or if a language, one lacking in the typical elements of alphabet, letter and word: Analogical language would be a language of relations, which consists of expressive movements, paralinguistic signs, breaths and screams (Deleuze 2004: 93). The analogical is a language of breaths and screams, a non-language of phatic commands, which enacts expression by virtue of the frisson struck between gestures of different types. Again back to the passage on synthesizers: Analogical synthesizers are modular, he writes, they establish an immediate connection between heterogeneous elements (95). So while digital synthesizers are integral, slicing up the world into masses of homogenous code atoms, analogical synthesizers work through modularity. What this means is that different elements, remaining relatively whole and heterogeneous to each other, are nevertheless able to interoperate immediately. They can touch each other directly, despite their differences. (One can begin to see why the elds of poststructuralism, deconstruction and semiotics were so

520 Alexander R. Galloway

inherently digital; as a rule they prohibit immediacy.) Whereas the digital requires and enlists an underlying homogeneity, the analogical requires an underlying heterogeneity. In the analogue paradigm, the stuff of the world remains unaligned, idiosyncratic, singular. These modules, thus, are not modules in the sense of standardised, recombinable parts, just as modular housing relies on prefabricated, repeatable materials. Rather, as modules they remain messy globs of dissimilar things. They only happen to interoperate because they have managed, by virtue of what Deleuze would call mutual deterritorialisation, to grow the necessary sockets that t into each other. Deleuzes famous example is the wasp and the orchid, two creatures, alike in almost no sense, that nevertheless couple up analogically. Although they are two, at the point of coupling the wasp and the orchid merge into one. Return briey to the mathematical theme. While Deleuze does not tell us directly, neither in the Postscript nor in the Francis Bacon book, one can infer the following: just as the digital means integration, the analogical means differentiation. Thus, while integration means area under a curve, differentiation or taking the derivative means the instantaneous slope of the tangent line. Instead of summing the area under the curve dened by f(x), one extrapolates a secondary function derived from the rst function, a secondary function consisting of a straight line tangential to any position x = a on the curve. It is slightly counter-intuitive then. Do not be fooled by the curves of integration, for it is still a question of solving via a multiplicity of regular slices, and hence it is digital. Likewise do not be fooled by the semantic similarity between the words differentiation and difference. Differentiation is an analogical event because it brings together the immediacy of two modular, and heterogeneous, spaces, (1) the space of the function curve and (2) the adjacent virtual space of all the tangent lines that can be derived from the curve. Heterogeneity has long been an attractive theoretical category, for Deleuze but also for twentieth-century Continental philosophy and Anglo-American cultural theory in general. And as we have just seen the analogue brings together heterogeneous elements into identity (an identity which, again, has nothing to do with homogeneity). I think there is a strong case to be made that Deleuze was and remained a philosopher of the analogue paradigm alone, and that the paradigm of the digital was only vaguely sketched out by him during his lifetime (except in its most visible form, metaphysics). The reasons for this are complex for they concern the history of philosophy and Deleuzes antagonistic relationship toward it, but as a kind of shorthand

Computers and the Superfold 521

we might posit the following: those who work in the tradition of metaphysics will tend to offer a digital philosophy; those who work in the tradition of immanence, as Deleuze did, will tend to offer an analogue philosophy. Indeed in many ways Deleuze is the analogical philosopher par excellence. Just as he described painting, the analogical art par excellence (Deleuze 2004: 95). What this brief excursion into digitality reveals is that the late Deleuze contains an original set of arguments about society and politics at the turn of the new millennium. We know Deleuze understood the world in 1968 the anabasis of desire, affective revolution, new schizophrenic subjects, molecular organisation, dispersive and rhizomatic structures, spatiality and topology instead of history, Leibniz instead of Hegel, Riemann instead of Einstein but the question remains whether he understood the world at the dawn of the new millennium. (This question has not been adequately explored thus far, although the work of someone like Bernard Stiegler is a notable exception.) Much has been said about Foucaults late turn to millennial politics, via his concepts of biopower and biopolitics, or Giorgio Agambens theorisation of todays state power, but too little credit has been given to Deleuze as a forecaster of the future world system. Part of the problem is that, barring the Postscript itself, there is no single book or text that stands out as a ready exemplar for Deleuzes analysis of millennial capitalism, just as Anti-Oedipus and A Thousand Plateaus provided a vision of middletwentieth-century capitalism. Such an exemplar needs to be reconstructed from fragments. Four texts will form the backbone of his analysis: the two pieces from 1990 bundled in Negotiations, Postscript on Control Societies and the interview with Negri titled Control and Becoming (Deleuze 1995b: 16982); paragraphs from an odd little piece called Having an Idea in Cinema (Deleuze 1998); and three or four pages from Deleuzes 1986 book Foucault (Deleuze 1988).6 Some of the relevant sections from the Postscript have already been outlined, so let us turn now to the ending of the Negri interview. The penultimate question and answer are what concern us:

[Foucault] was actually one of the rst to say that were moving away from disciplinary societies, weve already left them behind. Were moving toward control societies that no longer operate by conning people but through continuous control and instant communication... Compared with the approaching forms of ceaseless control in open sites, we may come to see the harshest connement as part of a wonderful happy past. The quest for universals of communication ought to make us shudder... Computer

522 Alexander R. Galloway

piracy and viruses, for example, will replace strikes and what the nineteenth century called sabotage (clogging the machinery)... The key thing may be to create vacuoles of noncommunication, circuit breakers, so we can elude control. (Deleuze 1995b: 174, 175)

Already it is evident how much of Deleuzes phrasing from the Negri interview overlaps with the text of the Postscript. Add now the passages from Having an Idea in Cinema, a text that derives from a lecture titled Quest-ce que lacte de création? given by Deleuze at La Fémis (Fondation européenne des métiers de limage et du son) on 17 May 1987 but published in 1990 the same year of the Postscript. Some of the relevant passages simply duplicate the same phrasing and language about Foucault that made it into the Postscript so there is no need to repeat them. But Having an Idea in Cinema also includes an important, off-hand remark that we must add to our accumulation of Deleuzes control quotations:

A control is not a discipline. In making freeways, for example, you dont enclose people but instead multiply the means of control. I am not saying that this is the freeways exclusive purpose, but that people can drive innitely and freely without being at all conned yet while still being perfectly controlled. This is our future. (Deleuze 1998: 18; translation modied)7

In an alternate transcription of the same lecture Deleuze included a few extemporaneous lines, and even mentions Minitel, the French teletext network that predates the web. This can be done completely differently too, he said about the regrouping of people around arrangements of ubiquitous control. It can be done through Minitel after all. Everything that you want whats astounding would be the forms of control (Deleuze 1987).8 Recall that the French contrôle carries stresses in meaning that are slightly different from the English control. Contrôle means control as in the power to inuence people and things, but it also refers to the actual administration of control via particular monitoring apparatuses such as train turnstiles, border crossings and check points. The notion, in English, of having to pass through passport control gets at the deeper meaning of the word. So when Deleuze talks about les sociétés de contrôle he means those kinds of societies, or alternately those localised places within the social totality, where mobility is fostered inside certain strictures of motion, where openings appear rather than disappear, where subjects (or for that matter objects) are liberated so long as they adhere to a variety of prescribed comportments.

Computers and the Superfold 523

In addition to this text and the two in Negotiations, a fourth text expands Deleuzes discussions of computer-based control, exploding them into an enigmatic tapestry of prognostications. Recall those notorious pages 923 and 1312 of Deleuzes late book on Foucault where he meditates on something called life resistance and a new mysterious construct called the superfold (an alluring designation to which he unfortunately never returns).9 First, consider the sections in which Deleuze proposes, but does not fully develop, a vision of life as living resistance:

When power... takes life as its aim or object, then resistance to power already puts itself on the side of life, and turns life against power... Life becomes resistance to power when power takes life as its object... When power becomes bio-power resistance becomes the power of life, a vital- power that cannot be conned within species, environment or the paths of a particular diagram... Is not life this capacity to resist force? (Deleuze 1988: 92, 93)

Then later, in the nal paragraphs of the books appendix, Deleuze broaches the question of genetics and the so-called third-generation machines (that is, computers and bioinformatics) that would gure prominently in the Postscript four years later. He wonders aloud about the death of man, as it was described in Foucault and Friedrich Nietzsche:

The question that continually returns is therefore the following: if the forces within man compose a form only by entering into a relation with forms from the outside, with what new forms do they now risk entering into a relation, and what new form will emerge that is neither God nor Man? This is the correct place for the problem which Nietzsche called the superman. (Deleuze 1988: 130)

In other words, what is the new conguration of man after the death of man (or, if you like, the subject after the death of the subject), and what had to happen in order to create such a new condition of life? Deleuzes answer:

Biology had to take a leap into molecular biology, or dispersed life regroup in the genetic code. Dispersed work had to regroup in third-generation machines, cybernetics and information technology. What would be the forces in play, with which the forces within man would then enter into a relation? It would no longer involve raising to innity or nitude but an unlimited nity, thereby evoking every situation of force in which a nite number of components yields a practically unlimited diversity of combinations. It would be neither the fold or the unfold that would constitute the active mechanism,

524 Alexander R. Galloway

but something like the Superfold, as borne out by the foldings proper to the chains of the genetic code, and the potential of silicon in third-generation machines... The forces within man enter into a relation with forces from the outside, those of silicon which supersedes carbon, or genetic components which supersede the organism... In each case we must study the operations of the superfold, of which the double helix is the best-known example. (Deleuze 1988: 1312)10 Scattered across the Postscript and these other citations is a new image of society and the self that cannot simply be reduced to Deleuzes previous tropes like the body without organs, the rhizome or even the virtual. This is a new image that involves, nay requires, the recognition of the computer as its central mitigating factor. Just as the fold was Deleuzes diagram for the modern subject of the baroque period, the superfold is the new active mechanism for life within computerised control society. The dividual and the superfold, in other words, have a special relationship with each other. A fold is always folded within a fold, like a cavern in a cavern, wrote Deleuze of the ontology depicted in Leibniz (in an effort to demonstrate how Leibnizs was not an atomism). The unit of matter, the smallest element of the labyrinth, is the fold, not the point which is never a part, but a simple extremity of the line (Deleuze 1993: 6). Although Deleuze does not specify things further, one can extrapolate that the superfold, being proper to the chains of the genetic code and the progeny of an unlimited diversity of combinations, would follow a diagrammatic logic of dispersive and distributive relations within networks, of iterative regress via computational recursion. Instead of the human coming into a relationship with itself (the baroque), the human comes into a relation with forces from the outside such as the silicon of the computer chip or exogenous factors from genetic engineering. The dividual therefore does not so much carry pleats in its soul, as Deleuze says of the baroque subject, but a tessellated, recombinant soul, if soul is still the proper word, forming and reforming across the metastable skein of the bioinformatic ecosystem. In fact Deleuzes argument is not an exotic one. In France gures like André Leroi-Gourhan and Bertrand Gille had already demonstrated how human beings coevolve with their exogenous technologies and techniques. And in North America gures like Lewis Mumford and Marshall McLuhan had made similar claims. (Indeed the nal paragraph of Deleuzes Foucault reads very much like Donna Haraways now famous Cyborg Manifesto, which while predating the book by one year was almost certainly unknown to Deleuze at the time.) Instead what

Computers and the Superfold 525

might be exotic about Deleuzes argument, or at least what makes it novel, is his mobilisation of the concept in terms of a diagram: the super fold, the double helix, a fractal topography not simply a folded one.11 The ultimate lesson to be learned from the Postscript is not so much a lesson about the subject or even society. The ultimate lesson is one about periodisation. For what Deleuze wishes to do in the essay, following Lyotard, Foucault and all the rest, is to assert the historical break. He wants to show us how everything has changed, indeed that the world of 1990 has itself changed from the world pre-1968 so dramatically as to be practically indistinguishable. The key thing is that were at the beginning of something new, he reminds us (Deleuze 1995b: 182). It is not particularly important whether one agrees or disagrees with the Deleuzian-Foucauldian periodisation from sovereign society through disciplinary society and then to control society. Periodisation itself is the important thing. And how deliciously ironic that in recent years periodisation seems to be appearing with increased frequency, an increased periodicity of periodisation. Indeed all this talk of the superfold is, by that very same measure, a kind of superperiodisation without end. For each new fold is a new historical break. First the fold, then the double fold, the triple, on up to the multiplicative folds of the superfold. Thus the task of historical thinking itself is implicated in Deleuzes Postscript, and as such has metastasised and reduplicated into a super state of recursive channels. The ultimate coup of control society is not so much the continuous inuence of the border crossing or the passport control, not so much data mining or facial recognition algorithms, but that it has eviscerated history, not by banning dissent, but by accelerating the opportunities and channels for critical thought to innity and therefore making it impossible to think historically in the rst place. Thus the central challenge within control society will be not simply to resist the various new nefarious control apparatuses, but to rescue history from its own consummation.

The Bachelors Fantasy: Autoimmunity in Theory

Alexander R. Galloway

A few years ago it was the schizophrenics, all those people walk - ing and talking with their hands- free headsets speaking loudly into the air. Now it is the drunks, those foggy heads stooping and stumbling down the sidewalk, attentive more to a text mes - sage than to the world around them. Human attention is a rare commodity. Its quality modulates according to different places and different times. Today attention tends to curl back on itself, corralled and kept from escaping into the outside world by the seduction of touch screens and handheld devices. Such screens bring telepresence, to be sure, as doorways into a communicative beyond. But these doorways are also mirrors, blocking the com - municative act and reecting the user back to himself or herself, the narcissist user who reaches out only to be touched, who posts only to read, who surfs only to rediscover the many iterations of my and you. systemic.4 Building on this characterization, I wish to continue Chows investigation into the self- referential nature of cultural and political theory by suggesting that theoretical discourse today is plagued by a form of autoimmune disorder. That is to say, certain kinds of cultural and political theory and I will qualify what and whom I mean shortly confront themselves as enemies, as some - thing that should be attacked. Or often, as we shall see, if they do not confront themselves directly, they face their own intellectual traditions and discursive contexts as hostile systems, as something to be infected, occupied, and ultimately disavowed. Like a hista - mine reaction or an autoimmune disorder, which stems from an overly aggressive response by the bodys immune system, thereby converting the self into its own pathogen, certain kinds of cultural and political theory today actualize a self- pathogenesis by positing the self as its own problem. Evoking autoimmune disorder in the realm of philosophy and theory, one cannot help but veer into the realm of metaphor. It is not my intention to downplay the rising importance of auto - immune diseases by positing some sort of analogous cultural dis - ease. Far from it. I wish to add new fuel to the sputtering attempts of late to allegorize theory via a symptomatology rooted in the material base of society, thereby foregrounding this new phenomenon rather than belittling it. The contagious, parasitical, or systemic sociotechnical landscape of the new millennium will gain new importance if it is revealed as such. And the state of theory today will be recast as an epiphenomenon of that conjuncture.

Virtual Theory For an introductory illustration, one may return to Chows discussion of the virtual in Age of the World Target, contrasting her treatment of the term with that of Gilles Deleuze and Jean Baudrillard. This will help illustrate each theorists methodology and show whether they ape the logic of self- referentiality and autoimmunity in their own thinking. Chow denes virtualization essentially as mediatization. 5 That is to say, she denes virtualization primarily in terms of the

• Camera Obscura

contemporary media spectacle: cable news networks like CNN, the advent of cameras on the noses of smart bombs, the way in which war has been turned into a video game in short, in terms of representation. The virtual is the realm of the mediatic. Hence, for Chow, the virtual will necessarily have a problematic relation - ship to the real, for as media spectacle it is at best divided from the real and at worst a horrible distortion of it. In this way Chow is participating in a long-standing tradition of aesthetic theory, one that establishes a normative yardstick for representation based on the various deviations or verisimilitudes between an original and its representation. (Close readers of Chow will want to compare this to her older work on untranslatability and a resistance against the image.)6 Contrast this with two different discussions of the virtual, those by Deleuze and Baudrillard. For his part, Deleuze does not talk about the virtual in opposition to the real.7 There is no metaphysical line dividing the real world from its many virtual avatars. The world is not metaphysical for Deleuze; the world is not divided. In fact, for Deleuze, the virtual is real. The virtual refers to a kind of transformation space available to actual things, and thus the virtual and the actual transpire within the same single plane of being. Virtualization means taking something out of its specicity as a solved fact and, in a way, thrusting it into an adjacent space of whatever kind. For example, to virtualize a parabola is to think of it in terms of its slopes, functions, thresholds, and singularities. Deleuze often conceives the virtual in terms of calculus: Taking the derivative of a function is a virtualization because a primary function (a curve, for example) establishes a relationship with a secondary function (the tangent line of the curve, which itself is a new function). Thus, given a curve, the set of all tangent lines would constitute a part of the virtual space of the curve. Likewise, Baudrillard denes the virtual less in terms of media spectacle, although spectacle indeed has its role to play, and more in terms of machinic and mathematical modeling of worlds.8 Simulation or the hyperreal are, for Baudrillard, a kind of virtualization of the real. Indeed, the semiotic fog of the culture industries permeates society so much that representation

The Bachelors Fantasy •

begins to supplant the real. Such a scenario is quite radical for Baudrillard, and it offers the possibility for an escape from the shackles of existing modes of social production and reproduction. Yet it is ultimately more cynical than that, for Baudrillards virtual refers not simply to media spectacle but to the world modeled, the world scanned, and the world planned. Hence, for Baudrillard, the virtuality of the real is dubbed a catastrophe because it means that the real has been planned, predicted, managed, and sculpted so much in advance that nothing contingent can ever take place. If the virtual in Deleuze constitutes the very conditions of the new, Baudrillard will sourly dismiss the virtual, indicting it as the per - fect crime.9 I animate this ctional debate between Chow and her French counterparts not so much to adjudicate the discussion but to carve into relief the structure of critique governing each thinker. Ironi - cally though likely by design Chows discussion of the virtual does not follow a structure of self- referentiality. Yet both Deleuze and Baudrillard, to varying degrees, do indeed follow this self- reexive structure. Deleuze apes the logic of systems theory, in which a system and its subsystems are always already codened here the actual entity (the parabola) and its virtualization (the parabolas solution set of all possible tangent lines). The same can be said for Baudrillard: any given entity is so completely overdetermined by the catastrophic thicket of context supporting it that it suffers a quick death, asphyxiation by self- referentiality. On this score, then, if one is to grant systems and systems theory a certain dominance in contemporary life, Deleuze and Baudrillard are unwittingly more allegorical of the present conditions of existence, while Chow is less so. To her credit, this leaves Chow with considerably greater distance from, and hence critical perspective on, the contemporary technosocial landscape.

The New Infrastructure of Self-Referentiality In Chow, then, self- referentiality in theory hints at a larger problem. She shows how there has been a preoccupation with differ - ence, particularly in the work of poststructuralism, but at the

same time an unwillingness to deal directly with the question of exclusion. Poststructuralism has always had a special relationship to alterity, she admits. But often this preoccupation with alter - ity obviates the very Other in question, leading to a situation in which differencing exists but without inclusion.10 Here, however, we are not simply talking about selfreferentiality or autoimmunity out of context. This is not a discussion disconnected from time or history. A longer discussion would need to tackle the question of modernism and its most emblem - atic gesture, self- reexivity. For is not the Proustian sentence, the Rietveld chair, or the Malevich square a high- water mark of selfreferentiality? Indeed, a historical survey of self- referentiality would need to go back further, to the dawn of the modern period itself, to the newfound autonomy granted to thinkers and doers, those who must reect on themselves absent the sight of God and in so doing produce new knowledge or exhibit their own agency in the world. Yet where self- reexivity in modernism appears as a grand deviation from conventional form (wherein form will ultimately gain its own apotheosis), self- referentiality in the information age appears not so much as a deviation from structure but as the nuts and bolts of structure itself. What used to be avant- garde is now frightfully quotidian. Self- referentiality has a particular currency today because of the fact that material apparatuses (techniques, infrastructures, discourses, behaviors, and so on) follow a logic of self- referentiality more and more at the level of their design and implementation. Todays sociotechnical landscape and the reader will have to take this somewhat on faith, barring a more thorough explanation, as it has already been the subject of considerable argument elsewhere in the work of everyone from Manuel Castells, to Michael Hardt and Antonio Negri, to Albert- László Barabási exhibits a logic not so much of mimesis or representa - tion but of the self- similar (for which the closest mode of gura - tion would not be mimesis but something more like metonymy or synecdoche).11 Consider the classical denition of a system from systems theory. Functionally, systems are dened as self-similar at any scale.

Like a fractal, for which any part no matter how small is statistically homologous to the whole, a system may be dened via reference to a localization of scale. Hence the human body is a system; but, scaling down, so too is the human circulatory system; and down again, so too is the cell; and likewise down to a molecule and beyond. Scaling up, one nds a structural self- similarity: now aggregated into groups, the human constitutes specic social systems, them - selves reaggregated into larger systems such as the nation- state or larger communities of afliation such as the indigenous- rights or transnational womens movements. Certainly systems have existed for a long time; what is special today is that the core of the new economy revolves around systems architectures: social networking software as systems of subsystems, search engines that extract value from attractors and clusters within network topologies, and lesharing software (like Bittorent) for which scaling up produces benets to the system rather than forcing bottlenecks or articial scarcity of resources. Thus theorys homology to the world carries particular urgency today, given the fact that self- referentiality is so thoroughly embedded into the mode of production. But this is not a conspiracy theory. It is ridiculous to insinuate that Deleuze or Baudrillard is colluding with the logic of the mode of production, even unknowingly. In their writings, both are quite vocally anticapitalist. So how does one read them? Is the symptomatic reading so thoroughly ingrained into critical methodology today that we have lost the ability to read in good faith? Might these kinds of texts have been written with autocritique already in mind, lapsing into a recursive hole of self- reection? Can we understand autoimmunity as theorys ultimate coping strategy: that any positive claim, always laid bare to its own deconstruction, must preemptively inoculate its own effectivity? Are there any more positive claims, or only the prevarications of quasi- claims? To read thinkers like this with any amount of good faith, one is forced into an odd editorial role: when one reads Deleuze on rhizomatic systematicity, one must silently murmur an amend - ment to the text on his behalf. One must silently add, But not that kind of rhizomatic systematicity the kind underpinning SAPs enterprise software products. In other words, when Deleuze

talks about assemblages and the virtual he clearly does not mean those kinds of assemblages and virtualities, the kinds that govern todays business infrastructure and thereby ultimately govern how production happens today. For what could be a better example of what Michel Foucault called the everyday fascisms denounced by Deleuze and Félix Guattari than the logic of the computer, a logic announcing far and wide that there are only bodies and languages, only entities to be captured and codes with which to manipulate them?12 To read Deleuze today, then, one is forced into an odd sort of disavowal. I give you the logic of the world, he tells us, but not that logic of the world. Such disavowals are as common as they are unusual. Allow me to step back a moment and offer a broader picture on the present state of affairs, with the hope of explaining, even partially, the current conundrum in which even these gures nd themselves. Whom do I mean? Consider the many scenes of self- referential disavowal in contemporary continental philosophy and critical theory. Con - sider, for example, Jacques Rancières writings on democracy. Consider how in Rancières Hatred of Democracy the greatest obstacle to democracy is democracy itself.13 We want real democracy, he writes, not this dreary democracy already in existence all around us. Or consider some of Rancières writings on aesthetics: the essence of unrepresentability has nothing to do with unrepresentability; or elsewhere, Rancière wants the emancipated spectator, but not that emancipated spectator, the one about which Antonin Artaud and Bertolt Brecht wrote. 14 Or consider Alain Badious writings about communism: no, of course Badiou does not want actually existing communism, for that was an abject failure, it was morally evil, and so on; he wants real communism, he wants the commu - nist hypothesis.15 Or even Badious writings on the event: yes, it is most virtuous to bring events into the world, but certainly not those events (the attack on the Twin Towers, Abu Ghraib, the Nazi death camps).16 Simon Critchleys writings on religion demonstrate the same self- referential conundrum. In the wake of modern secular - ism, one no longer seeks God, he suggests, but one nevertheless still

seeks the faith of the faithless: faith, but not that faith.17 Or Reza Negarestani, who calls for openness, but not that openness (the kind promulgated by economic liberalism). 18 Susan Buck- Morss also illustrates nicely theorys scene of disavowal in her recent book on Hegel and Haiti. She proposes that one rescu[e] the idea of universal human history from the uses to which white domina - tion has put it.19 So she wants to claim the universal, but not that universal, the one that has oppressed us (and others) for so long. Many other gures reenact this same disavowal. For instance, Catherine Malabou falls prey to the circular logic of disavowal. She calls for open networks, but not those open networks; she elevates the categories of change and metamorphosis (under the aegis of plasticity), but not that kind of change, the kind wrought by bourgeois capitalism, the kind that trumpets in triumph that all that is solid melts into air, the kind that brings into existence subjects that are interminably precarious and exible. 20 Across these many authors Rancière, Badiou, Critchley, Negarestani, Buck- Morss, and Malabou one witnesses an inability to speak in terms that are resolutely incompatible with the present state of affairs. Instead, through a kind of autoinfection, they ventriloquize their own environment, inecting it with an affective yearning that someday, somehow it might all be just a little different, even as it is the same: the world, but not that world. The sentiment is there, but the critique is not yet fully formed. One might summarize philosophys autoimmune disorder via the following logic: assert the goal of maintaining a thing or state of affairs, but only if that thing or state of affairs is entirely rescued and returned to what it should be. A grammarian might observe that such disavowals are an example of the demonstrative adjective, used in a pejorative sense (that, as in the world, but not that world; Latin benets from having a separate adjective specically for this purpose: iste, ista, istud). In general, it is symptomatic of the decline in political efciency today. It indicates a decline in the inability to make trenchant political judgments. In short, few today are willing to put forth a positive political claim, free from all the hemming and hawing of disavowal and compromise.

The Bachelors Fantasy The root question, then, is one of desire. An age- old political question returns anew: Do we really know what we want? Is the goal to achieve a deviation from the state of affairs, or is the goal to return to what already exists, warmed over and reenchanted? As Stanley Cavell has indicated in his study of the remar - riage lm, this logic has no better expression than in the bedroom comedies of the classical Hollywood period. 21 While these lms predate the information age, they seem to predict it, at least at the level of logical structure. Shall We Dance (dir. Mark Sandrich, US, is one of the better entries in this category, not least for its propensity to reveal the representational apparatus from the protocinematic ip book and the skipping gramophone to the Ginger Rogers mannequin and her dancing garrison of masked doubles but even more for its ability to reshufe the very coordinates of desire such that the various unions and trysts are brought about in a false way only to be revealed as true in the end: But how will we ever get a divorce? Eureka, well get married rst! Yet it is in Alfred Hitchcocks Mr. and Mrs. Smith (US, where the basic structure of philosophys autoimmune disorder is best displayed (g. ). And taking a cue from Hitchcock, one might give the disorder a proper name: the bachelors fantasy. Recall the lms story line: due to a clerical mix- up at city hall, a husband discovers that he and his wife were technically never married, despite having lived as man and wife for several years already. To the husband, Mr. Smith (Robert Montgomery), this is received as a stroke of good luck, fodder for a bit of romantic spice, as he is now free again to court and pursue his own wife as if she were an unwed woman, his mistress perhaps. Hence the fundamental structure of Mr. Smiths fantasy: he wants to pursue his wife, but only because she is not his wife. Hitchcock has covered this ground on more than one occasion, perhaps most famously in Vertigo (US, To be sure, the implications of the man- woman arrangement appear to be rather complicated if not odious, particularly to any kind of feminist project, as the very essence of woman is assumed to be that thing that

The Bachelors Fantasy •

is essentially manipulable the thing that is able to be sculpted into the ultimate object of male desire. The man really does want to court his own wife, except in his fantasy she has a bigger bust, smaller waist, different hair color, and so on. But this man is no philanderer, mind you; it is always still his wife he wants to court. Fantasy is often understood in a commonsense way as the desire for another object, as ones playful daydreams for some lost thing of desire. Hitchcock, however, shows that Mr. Smiths fantasy does not work in the same way. Mr. Smiths desire has an object, his wife, but that object only becomes such via a fantasy structure of imagining that she appears in another form altogether (a strum - pet, his school sweetheart, or what not). Acquiring a real mistress would never titillate Mr. Smith in the same way. The structure of fantasy cannot be short- circuited simply by skipping over to the ultimate object of desire. Mr. Smith does not want a mistress; he wants his wife, he wants the same person, even insomuch as she must be transformed into a kind of nonwife. Thus the structure of Mr. Smiths fantasy is one of postponement and asynthesis, never one of direct consummation. This is why desire is always a striptease, never a pornography; only the drives can be a pornography. And perhaps the structure is a partial explanation for why fantasy and desire have always held an important place in feminist discourse, even if the specter of male fantasy seems to complicate things a great deal.

What Should Criticism Be? The accusation should now be clear: the structure of political critique mentioned previously with Badiou and Critchley and all the rest follows this same fantasy logic. In short, we are all Mr. Smith now. Rancière wants democracy, but not that democracy, the one he has been living within all his life. Badiou wants communism, but not that communism, the one promulgated by Stalin, or in another way today by Hu Jintao. Our most advanced political critiques are locked inside a logic of postponement and asynthesis. The utopian resolution is held up as perfect, only to be revealed

• Camera Obscura

as a kind of facsimile of the present state of affairs. No synthesis is possible, only a perpetual postponement. Is it not the very same logic of spectacle capitalism seen time and time again in the coda to Lewis Carrolls Alice in Wonderland, L. Frank Baums The Wizard of Oz, or other artifacts of popular culture: to discover that it was all a dream (and thank God for that); to exhale nally in the security of knowing that ones innermost yearnings are really yearn - ings for the comforts of normal life to continue undisturbed? Because of this we are living today through a curious phase in the history of philosophy. This phase may be characterized as both gnostic and phenomenological, two rather strange bed - fellows that nevertheless align toward each other in interesting ways. The gnostic inuence preaches that, as individuals, we are all marooned here temporarily in this profane world. The phe - nomenological inuence preaches that in order to be liberated we need the essence of x to shine forth in what it is. It is a uni - versalization of the central paradox driving Heideggers famous essay on technology that the essence of x is nothing like x. Of course the point is not that any or all of the aforementioned writers are gnostics (like Baudrillard was) or phenomenologists (like Heidegger was) but rather that, when examined at the scale of discourse, the structure of these collective arguments can be seen to follow a gnostic- phenomeno- logic. They aim to rescue mundane reality by allowing it to shine forth in what it is. One might even say (to be least sympathetic) that today there exists among many of our most advanced, progressive theorists a refusal to engage in real critique a desire, in essence, for the status quo. Across this overview of contemporary theory, albeit brief and synoptic, I have posed and to a certain extent answered one of the central questions in any kind of intellectual endeavor: What should criticism be? Should criticism essentially follow the path of phenomenology (let something shine forth in what it is) or the path of gnosticism (this temporary profane world shall be transcended in the end)? With due respect to my betters, I propose that criticism as phenomenology is no criticism at all. Criticism that seeks to allow something in chrysalis to be reborn as what it is already is no criti-

The Bachelors Fantasy •

cism at all. And likewise criticism as gnosticism is no criticism at all. Criticism that preaches a messianic timescale of redemption from this profane world is no criticism at all. Intellectual history proffers two sources for the concept of critique, the Kantian one and the Marxian one. Immanuel Kants notion of critique grants freedom of thought to the Enlightenment individual, but only under the strictures of allegiance to the sovereign. With deference to Frederick II of Prussia, Kant parrots the following dictum governing the balance between public and private discourse: Argue as much as you like and about whatever you like, but obey!22 The Kantian tradition of critique is thus a compromise between modern free thought and obedience to the law. Marxian critique, on the other hand, while also relying on scientic reason to pierce through the various mystications and dogmas of the world, grants no such deference to the powers that be. Instead, Marxian critique is motivated by a political commitment rooted in history and materiality. It is that lost art, Marxian dialectics, that proposes a logic totally incompatible with both gnosticism and phenomenology. In contrast to the gnostic and phenomenological versions of critique, dialectical criticism says let something dis appear through a synthetic encounter with its opposite. If phenomenol - ogy is a return, and gnosticism is a transcendence, dialectics calls for a true negation. Yet the task at hand is not to restore the true criticism, for that would simply represent a return to the bachelors fantasy: critique, but not that critique. And certainly there is a danger here, that the dialectic is a kind of autoimmunity logic writ large, as self and other are endlessly negated and alienated in service to their own self- realization. Yet an advantage of Marxian critique over the Kantian, gnostic, and phenomenological variants is that it aims to revolutionize the current state of affairs, not to reform it piece - meal. Likewise, the Marxian concept of critique aims to abolish the state of the situation via reference to the suppressed material fact. The liberal bourgeoisie are the ones who say: yes capitalism, but not that capitalism. Marxist critics are more likely to slice through such mealymouthed disavowals: not that capitalism, nor any other variety.

To Abstain from the Principle of Sufcient Critique So where does this leave us? Recall the chicken scene in Ernst Lubitschs lm Bluebeards Eighth Wife (US, another of the great comedies of the classical Hollywood period (fig. ). The scene takes place at the exit of a sanatorium between a doctor and his patient, a wealthy businessman who, after being driven to his wits end by the crashing stock market, had been convinced he was a chicken. In a moment of levity the doctor saunters with his patient, now cured of being a chicken, out the doorway of the hospital and ushers him toward the street beyond. Goodbye profes - sor, and thank you a thousand times, the ex- chicken says to the doctor, Ill never forget that terrible morning when I ew into the kitchen and said to the cook, Ana, where are the noodles? Quick, make soup out of me! Strange what the stock market can do to one. But moments later on the street the supposedly healthy businessman, upon reading newspaper headlines announcing a new drop in commodities prices, can utter but one full- throated crow: cock- a- doodle- do!23 Lubitsch neatly evokes the straitjacket structure of subject formation that has produced the current philosophical conun - drum. The bachelors fantasy achieves its goals by shackling dis - course to one of two options: one is either living healthily within the sphere of representation, or ones mental stability has been shattered by the vicissitudes of the market. Either businessman or chicken, either successful capitalist or madman; no other options exist. Supplementing this with Mr. Smiths fantasy, one can see the peculiar logic that governs the state of self- referential disavowal: not those chicken capitalists, we want the non- chicken capitalists. But if one pauses for a moment in order to bracket this self- defeating logic, it is simple to see that the most important question is the one that is never asked. The most important question is how one might y the coop entirely and start anew. One must abstain from such a principle of sufcient cri - tique (to parody François Laruelle); one must abstain from critique of the political as a hypothesis based in Mr. Smiths male fantasy.24 Yet such a suggestion is not simply run- of- the- mill anxious liberalism, to kill ones idols, or to shrug off all kinds of fantasy as mere

The Bachelors Fantasy •

illusion. The point is not that living within representation is bad or that Critchley or Rancière should bracket their fantasies and get real. In a sense, the point is that they are not phantasmal enough. A particular example might help illustrate the kind of intellectual arc sought here. Consider the trio of books published over the last decade by Hardt and Negri: Empire, Multitude, and Commonwealth.25 While these books have elicited numerous responses both small and large, minor and major, there is an essential tension at the heart of the trilogy that bears on the present conversation. On the one hand, the second volume, Multitude, in particular suffers from an acute case of the bachelors fantasy. Hardt and Negri state unambiguously that they seek a return to democracy, only not that democracy, the kind existing in Italy, the United States, France, or elsewhere. So an iteration of the autoimmunity logic certainly lingers in these texts. Yet at the same time, by the end of the trilogy, they arrive trenchantly, unapologetically, and unironically at a number of purely positive conditions of fact: love, happiness, joy, and an end to evil and injustice. In a similar vein, one might hold up the various global occupation movements and their refrain of having no demands as a form of political consciousness resolutely contrary to the bachelors fantasy. The Occupy Wall Street movement as but one moment in a set of larger geopolitical upheavals spanning Tunisia, Egypt, Greece, Spain, Chile, the UK, Israel, and elsewhere is notoriously ununied in its message, lacking leaders and specic political ideologies. Yet in this very withdrawal from having demands, in this implicit rejection of the existing channels of political mediation (the ballot box, the representative, the mass media, the manifesto, the political party), the movement bypasses the autoimmune instinct. The movement does not want to x the current demo - cratic system; it wants to leave it behind, proclaiming that another world is possible. Such a world, however and this is crucial is not to be found in the kingdom of heaven or via some return to a lost origin. It is found in this park, this town square, this build - ing, this patch of grass, these lands that, once occupied, will never again be the same. Thus on the one hand we must certainly continue to oper-

Whence often arise the temptations of the militant uto - pias to drop out and withdraw completely from the world system. The ascetics, the cynics, the subtractivists, the back- to- the- landers, the withdrawalists all others are mere reformers, the middle- management product testers for tomorrows upgrade. But traps linger here as well. One might heed the advice of Fredric Jameson when he reminds us that the dropout fantasies and the so- called enclave utopias are ideological in their own right and emerge as the result of specic historical situations. 28 Their utility is limited and should be understood provisionally if at all. This is why the new global mass movements are so valuable. They indicate that the solution will lie elsewhere not in a cynical withdrawal from the world system but in an occupation of its very heart. The Occupy movements suggest that the solution will lie somewhere buried beneath the values that are anathema to todays world system: care, truth, work, sincerity, sacrice, nothingness, morality, love, discipline, peace, and even death. Following their lead, todays cultural and political theorists would be wise to devote serious attention to their own allegorical conditions. Aping the principles of recursion and self- reection endemic to the network architectures of the economic base, such cultural and political theory is still plagued by an autoimmune disorder. Until it con - fronts this condition head on, it will always view itself as something of an enemy that must be attacked. In other words, the reexive pathogenesis of theory, its own autoinfection, poses a formidable challenge to the future viability of critical thought. Until this is addressed, it will be difcult to summon, and more difcult to satisfy, that most basic question underlying all progressive move - ments: What do we want?

Introspection is often necessary in academic work, not simply concerning the objects of the mind but also the actual manner in which intellectual work is done. This typically comes under the heading of methodology. Yet the meaning of methodology is not always clear, particularly within the so-called theory disciplines that span Marxism, feminism, poststructuralism, psychoanalysis, and related elds. Some prefer the self-serving and somewhat vain conviction that theory and methodology are one and the same pursuit. Hence doing theory would seem to preempt the thorny exercise of methodological introspection, rendering it moot. Why speak of method when theory is nothing but method? Why worry about other tasks when theory is king? Yet the reality of higher education contradicts such pat conclu - sions. In fact, academic halls are teeming with a vast array of di erent research methods, from the positivistic expediency of quantitative investigation, to the staging of ethnographic interviews, to the narrative reductions of historiography, to the various instrumentalized strains of hermeneutics such as the Marxist reading, the feminist reading, or the psychoanalytic reading.

In other words, methodology today has a distinctly liberal prole. For every taste, there is a method to match. For every predilection, there is a satisfaction to be had. In order to be successful today, a student or scholar must internalize the many options and enact them appropriately given the task at hand; this method for that problem, followed by a new method for the next. In this sense, methodology today is often more a question of appropriateness than existential t, more a question of personal style than universal context, more a question of pragmatism than unwavering conviction. But appropriateness is a thorny business, and not everyone agrees on matters of taste. Many methodological discussions devolve into a sort of popularity contest. Who advocates what method and for what purpose? Which general equivalent trumps all others? Is it sexuality, or is it class, or is it the logos, the archive, the gaze, desire, play, excess, singularity, resis - tance, or perhaps life itself, elevating one methodological formation above all others in a triumphant critique (to end all future critique)? A contradiction thus emerges: the historical forces that gener - ate liberal ecumenicalism are the same forces that strive to canalize and entrain such heterogeneity under a single symbolic order. The liberal prole of contemporary scholarly methodology is thus a kind of method-e ect in which diversity of method is simultaneously asserted and withheld. The situation is even more puzzling, however, as many humanities disciplines have in recent years marked a shift away from qualitative methods, as diverse and multitudinous as they are, in favor of more quantitative and empirical research techniques. In an apparent rebu to methodological ecumenicalism, the positivistic expediency of quantitative research has tended to out ank other methods within Western modernity, as todays debate around digital humanities again makes clear. Appeals to empirical verication, to the reduction of complexity into simplicity, to the principles of repeatability and objectivity, to the sequential logic of the syllogism or the deductive argumentappeals, in short, to the paradigm of Enlightenment reason handed down since the Baroque turn of Descartes, Kepler, Galileo, and Leibnizhave gradually edged out all the others. A liberal array of possibilities galvanized to a single methodological tendencybut why, and how? Perhaps the very question of method refers to that moment in history when knowledge becomes production, when knowledge loses its absolute claims to immanent ecacy, when knowledge ceases being intuitive and must be legitimized via recourse to some kind of metadiscourse. The ability to speak authoritatively is not a newfound right bestowed on humanity in the modern period, as recounted in the various narratives

A cultural worker who deploys such methods is little more than a lesser Amazon or a lesser Equifax. A century ago, capital had a monopoly on the physical materiality of production. Now it has a monopoly on the immaterial sphere of informatic commerce. Industry has nally moved into the realm of intellectual labor, and by most reports it is excelling beyond all expectations. Many scholarly researchers must therefore face a startling fact: the corporate sector sim - ply has far superior data reserves at its disposal. Thus, in the information society, the scholar of information will forever be trapped in a decit of resources, playing catch-up behind the scads of mathematics PhDs on sta at Google. Never before in history have immaterial and informatic assets been so closely intertwined with capital. But beyond the challenge of unequal talent and resources is the question of critical ecacy. Is it appropriate to deploy positivistic techniques against those self-same positivistic techniques? In a former time, such criticism would not have been valid or even necessary. Marx was writing against a system that laid no specic claims to the apparatus of knowledge production itselfeven if it was fueled by a persistent and pernicious form of ideological misrecognition. Yet, today the state of a airs is entirely reversed. The new spirit of capitalism is found in brainwork, self-measurement and self-fashioning, perpetual critique and innovation, data creation and extraction. In short, doing capitalist work and doing intellectual workof any variety, bourgeois or progressiveare more aligned today than they have ever been.1 Hence there appears something of a moral crisis concerning the very validity of scholarly methodologies. Such methods are at best underfunded and impotent cousins to the new algorithmic industries and at worst unknowing shills for that same system of canalization and debasement. The question is no longer can we use the masters tools to take down the masters house? Today the question is can we still use our own tools now that the master has taken them up?

Beyond simply asserting or describing the existence of a certain social, cultural, and economic paradigm, beyond simply moralizing about it or fomenting some kind of reinvigorated hermeneutics of suspicion fashioned to debunk it, I wish to shift tone and provide a more detailed picture of the contemporary landscape. How and when were the seeds of the digital universe planted? What are the historical conditions that had to be developed in order for the concept of the digital humanities to make sense? When and how did the creation and recombination of knowledge gain its distinctly liberal prole in which each thinker may pursue his or her own autonomous goals? Why would such an arrangement be benecial for the extraction of surplus-value? The aim here is thus to explore the history of digital society in classic Foucauldian fashion, to explore some of the conditions of possibility for cybernetic society. Norbert Wiener invented the science of cybernetics, of course, but what conditions of possibility had to have been invented in years prior for him to be able to innovate? Claude Shannon put forth a new model of information science, but what conditions of possibility had to exist already for the world to be conceived as information in the rst place? Thus I o er a slightly di erent history of cybernet - ics not to overturn the existing histories, but to extend and reorient them. This supplementary history starts earlier in the twentieth century (with important additional precedents in the nineteenth that we must skip for the moment) and continues to the present day, relying on sources drawn from media, culture, technology, and philosophy. The basic argument I wish to propose here is that the liberal hue of contemporary methodologywith quantitative positivism serving as the governor of the rainbow coalitionis chie y due to a single historical phenomenon that has taken place over roughly the last century. Taking a page from the French collective Tiqqun, we might label this historical phenomenon the cybernetic hypothesis. Such a hypothesis refers to a specic epistemological regime in which systems or networks combine both human and nonhuman agents in mutual communication and command. Along with the many related elds that parallel cyberneticsnetwork sciences like ecology, systems theory, and graph theory; the sciences of economic decision such as game theory and rational choice theory; information science and signal processing; behaviorism, cognitivism, and the post-Freudian sciences of the subjectthe cybernetic hypothesis has come to dominate the production and regulation of society and culture.2 Tiqqun views the cybernetic hypothesis as a new kind of social management involving both human and nonhuman assets. Crystalline Space

In through what he labeled a strictly numerical process, the English mathematician Lewis Richardson proposed a massive chess game to span the continents, a system to predict weather via a cellular space of distributed meteorological sensors (g. ). He used the term lat - tice to describe this new device, borrowing a word from crystallography. Then, making a dramatic conceptual leap that would later in uence John von Neumann and the science of cellular automata, Richardson proposed that these many sprawling intercontinental cells coordinate to form a single computational system.

[W]e take a piece of paper ruled in large squares, like a chess - board, and let it represent a map. The lines forming the squares are taken as meridians and parallels of longitudean unusual thing in map projection. Next, we lay down the convention that all numbers written inside a square relate to the latitude and longitude of its center. [...] It is seen that pressure and momentum alternate in a pattern, which is such that, if a chessboard had been used, the pressures would all appear on the red squares, and the momenta all on the white ones, or vice versa. (Richardson )

The computational framework extends vertically too, rising through four distinct atmospheric layers. His language is that of complex and nonlinear systems, bor - rowed, in particular, from thermodynamics. It is the language of eddy movements, laminar stresses, air viscosity, turbulence, heat ows, and conductivity. Using the same discourse that would later in uence theorists like Gilles Deleuze and Félix Guattari, Richardson includes a whole section on heterogeneity and speaks in terms of the molecular and molar levels. He discusses the complexity of interactions between layers and the turbulence that results. Then, with a wink, Richardson adds a little rhyme to help remember it all: We realize thus that: big whirls have little whirls that feed on their velocity, and little whirls have lesser whirls and so on to viscosity ().

Problems and Proposals

The debate over digital humanities is thus properly framed as a debate not simply over this or that research methodology but over a general regime of knowledge going back several decades at least. Given what we have established thus farthat digital methods are at best a benign part of the zeitgeist and at worst a promulgation of late twentieth-century computationalismlet me end by itemizing a series of problems and challenges that anyone partaking in digital methods must consider.

Hegemony, Recapitulation, and Symmetry

Given the hegemonic status of computers in contemporary lifea position endorsed by everyone from Kevin Kelly and Thomas Friedman to Manuel Castells and Michael Hardt and Antonio Negrito propose computercentric research methodologies is to propose that the humanities follow a trend toward normalization with the dominant rather than of di erentiation from it. This will present a problem to certain intellectual endeavors that value deviation over normalization, heterodoxy over orthodoxy.
